title: Sima Guang Didn't Smash a Vat? The Earliest Record Came 30 Years After He Died
description:
A 1920s reader calls the vat "five or six feet tall"; a 2015 TV collector doubted the Song could fire one that big. History of Song (1345): jar (weng); Shao Bowen (1132): jar; earliest so far: monk Huihong, late Northern Song. Su Shi's life of Sima Guang omits small matters. Shuowen: gang (vat) was a long-necked pot; a 17th-c. Jingdezhen brush pot: a basin; late-Qing/Republican textbooks swapped in vat; the first "smash the vat" may be a 1933 Shen Bao ad. Song capital rain rites used jars; "Please step into the jar" is in Sima Guang's own Zizhi Tongjian. A jar: closed. Did it happen: open.

Texts: Daizhige, Wikisource; scholars via Zhonghua Book Co.; 2015 show via The Paper, paraphrased; "we think"/"I guess" are our views.

AI art; historical figures are cartoons, not likenesses.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (redone 2026-10-25, new rules)

chapters.monk-desk: Around 1120: a monk writes the scene down
chapters.su-writes: Su Shi writes his life, but not this part

sg101.text: You surely read: Sima Guang smashes the vat.

sg102.text: But in 2015, a collector on TV said it was fake: the Song couldn't fire a vat that big.

sg103.text: In the 1920s, a Shanghai publisher put out a reader for schoolchildren.

sg104.text: In it, a child falls into a water vat; Sima Guang bangs it with a stone, and water flows out.

sg105.text: It adds: "This vat is really big, a full five or six feet tall."

sg106.text: It even asks: why didn't clever Sima Guang care for that vat?

sg107.text: Still not the oddest part: a late Northern Song monk wrote it, and said one thing was common in the capital.

sg108.text: In the 17th century, a porcelain brush pot pictured it too: how was the vessel drawn?

sg109.text: This file traces the vat book by book, from the 1920s back to the Song.

sg110.text: Did Sima Guang really smash a vat?

sg201.text: The official History of Song, finished by the Yuan in 1345, uses a different word.

sg202.text: Kids play in a yard; one climbs a jar, slips, falls in the water;

sg203.text: everyone runs; Sima Guang breaks the jar with a stone, water bursts out, the kid lives.

sg204.text: Two "jars" (weng) in one short passage, and no "vat" (gang).

sg205.text: This stopped me too. And the "smashed a vat at seven" you grew up on?

sg206.text: In the History of Song, at seven he hears the Zuo Zhuan, retells it at home;

sg207.text: from then on, books never left his hands; he forgot hunger and cold.

sg208.text: The jar line comes later, with no year attached.

sg209.text: The book came some 320 years after Sima Guang turned seven.

sg211.text: Another Southern Song biography skips it: Zuo Zhuan at seven, then he takes office.

sg212.text: So no surviving official biography has it. Then where did it come from?

sg213.text: Further back, in 1132, Shao Bowen's Wenjian Lu already had it.

sg214.text: His version: a kid falls in a big water jar; Sima Guang breaks it with a stone; the kid gets out.

sg215.text: Shao pairs it with another boyhood tale:

sg216.text: Wen Yanbo used water to float a ball out of a hole.

sg217.text: He adds: the discerning saw rare kindness and wit in both boys.

sg218.text: Over 200 years before the History of Song, and also a jar.

sg219.text: But was Shao Bowen the first?

sg301.text: No. About ten years earlier, around 1120, the monk from the opening had already written it.

sg302.text: He's Huihong; his notes, Lengzhai Yehua, are the earliest record found so far.

sg303.text: By then Sima Guang had been dead some 30 years.

sg304.text: Could this earliest record say vat?

sg305.text: No. He writes: a big jar stands in the yard; a kid climbs it and falls in;

sg306.text: Sima Guang knocks the jar with a stone; water jets from a hole; the kid's OK.

sg307.text: Unlike Shao Bowen, he writes not "broke" but "knocked a hole." Did he give the age?

sg308.text: No. Just that Sima Guang was little, losing baby teeth, about when you lost your first front tooth.

sg309.text: That one thing, he noted too:

sg310.text: The capital and Luoyang had lots of jar-hitting pictures.

sg311.text: I can see it: a story so popular it's painted and seen all around the capital.

sg312.text: A Song catalog called the book not very reliable.

sg313.text: So did Huihong make this one up?

sg314.text: A scholar judged it broadly credible, not made up by Huihong;

sg315.text: Shao Bowen lived in Luoyang, his family close to Sima Guang's, and he recorded it too.

sg316.text: And in 1188, a Southern Song encyclopedia copied this entry, noting: from Lengzhai Yehua.

sg317.text: Its heading: "Picture of Striking the Jar."

sg318.text: Did people close to Sima Guang write about it?

sg401.text: One man should have written it above all: Su Shi. He said he'd known Sima Guang 20 years.

sg402.text: After Sima Guang died, Su Shi wrote a long account of his life.

sg403.text: He knew Sima Guang's life best, he said, so he kept to major events.

sg404.text: Remember the Zuo Zhuan at seven in the History of Song? It's from here, almost verbatim.

sg405.text: But the jar right after it isn't in this piece, nor on Sima Guang's tomb stele. Why?

sg406.text: His last note: the rest, unrelated to the realm's order and safety, he left out.

sg407.text: A rescue? Either he didn't know or saw no need.

sg408.text: Let me be clear: this can't prove it didn't happen.

sg409.text: Writing a chancellor's life, would you put in his childhood rescue?

sg410.text: I probably wouldn't either. But in the same long piece, Su Shi did record something else:

sg411.text: Crowds stopped Sima Guang, crying: don't return to Luoyang; stay, aid the throne, save the people.

sg412.text: "Save the people": remember those words for now.

sg413.text: Are the pictures Huihong noted still around?

sg501.text: We found none. The earliest image we can see is the brush pot from the opening:

sg502.text: 17th-century Jingdezhen blue-and-white, now at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

sg503.text: The vessel I asked about is painted as a big wide-mouthed basin, patterned outside.

sg504.text: A kid by the basin lifts his hands high; three or four run off.

sg505.text: The Song writers' jar got a wider mouth on porcelain.

sg506.text: I stared at that photo long: it's already the vat you picture.

sg507.text: So what did the word gang, "vat," first mean?

sg508.text: The Eastern Han dictionary Shuowen Jiezi, per Xu Kai's edition and Duan Yucai's notes: gang was a long-necked clay pot.

sg509.text: The Song had the word too: twice in the History of Song, both on wine;

sg510.text: once a gift of ten vats of wine, once officials scorned as wine vats and rice bags.

sg511.text: No Song writer of this story we found used it.

sg512.text: And what we call a vat today is wide-mouthed; small mouth, big belly is a jar.

sg513.text: Picture a pickle pot at home: small mouth, big belly. That's a jar.

sg514.text: So when did the story's jar become a vat?

sg601.text: A scholar combed late-Qing and Republican school textbooks and found that's when vat replaced jar.

sg602.text: Textbooks had "strike the vat" or "knock the water vat," but not yet "smash."

sg603.text: The opening reader titles that section "Sima Guang Breaks a Vat, Saves a Life."

sg604.text: Guess what the section before it is?

sg605.text: It's the Wen Yanbo ball tale Shao Bowen paired it with; even the "tree hole" matches a Southern Song encyclopedia.

sg606.text: It keeps the Song writers' order but swaps the jar for a vat; it's the earliest vat we opened.

sg607.text: My guess: the version you read as a kid came down this line; at "five or six feet tall," I truly laughed.

sg608.text: And when did "smash the vat" first appear?

sg609.text: According to a scholar's article, the earliest found so far may be a 1933 ad in the Shen Bao.

sg610.text: It sold a picture set of model children's tales; number 13: "Sima Smashes the Vat."

sg611.text: The scholar thinks that's likely when "Sima Guang Smashes the Vat" became its name.

sg612.text: Name set, vat set. Then someone used this vat to question the whole story.

sg701.text: That's the collector from the start. Does "the Song couldn't fire a vat that big" hold up?

sg702.text: A scholar replied: judging the original "jar" by the later "vat" just doesn't fit.

sg703.text: I find that spot-on: as you've heard so far, of the Song and Yuan people who wrote this, none used vat.

sg704.text: So did the Song have big jars?

sg705.text: In the Xining era, 1068 to 1077, while Sima Guang still lived, the capital had a great drought;

sg706.text: a Song notebook says each lane set out a big jar of water to pray for rain.

sg707.text: The History of Song's rites treatise adds: in a summer drought in Xining 10, the court issued a rain rite: dozens of lizards in jars.

sg708.text: Neither says how big the jars were; what's certain is that the capital prayed for rain with jars.

sg709.text: The opening reader says five or six feet tall, but none of the Song or Yuan texts we read gives the jar's height.

sg710.text: Any record of a jar that could hold an adult?

sg801.text: Yes, a famous one: the idiom "Please step into the jar."

sg802.text: A cruel Tang official proposed using a big jar to force confessions; another did so, then invited the first one in.

sg803.text: You've surely heard this idiom; but have you wondered which book it's in?

sg804.text: The Zizhi Tongjian. A book Sima Guang himself edited, presented in 1084.

sg805.text: It happened in 691, over 300 years before Sima Guang was born.

sg806.text: Another in the History of Song: Yue Fei, not a month old; a Yellow River flood; his mother rides a jar ashore with him.

sg807.text: That's a birth legend, not archaeological proof; but we think that to Song people, a jar holding an adult was nothing odd.

sg808.text: So next time you hear "the Song had no big jars," ask them to look in Sima Guang's own book.

sg809.text: Remember the opening reader's question? Why didn't clever Sima Guang care for that vat?

sg810.text: Because by the record, he never smashed a vat: it was a jar.

sg811.text: Interestingly, mainland China's third-grade classical text uses weng, jar, again; yet people still say "smash the vat."

sg812.text: But did he really save a child when he was little?

sg901.text: The records can't answer that; what they show is how Song people saw it.

sg902.text: Huihong's entry is titled "Means of Saving a Life": the skill of rescuing.

sg903.text: In the Southern Song, a self-cultivation book included it, under "helping others."

sg904.text: Song readers saw kindness in it, not just cleverness. So is it tied to Sima Guang's later fame?

sg905.text: Remember the words Su Shi recorded? "Save the people."

sg906.text: To a scholar, the tale spreading only after Sima Guang died is no fluke, given that fame;

sg907.text: As for whether it really happened, that scholar says: there's no way to know anymore. I read that line twice.

sg908.text: So this file: one page closed, one page still open.

sg909.text: In your childhood version: vat, jar, or other? Tell me below.

sg910.text: This channel sticks to the records; subscribe to open files with us.
